name: Linear A
signs: c. 90 syllabic signs plus logograms and numerals

claims.text: Linear A was used on Crete from c. 1800 to 1450 BC.
Linear B was adapted from Linear A.
The language recorded is not Greek.
Approximate phonetic values can be assigned from Linear B correspondences.
The underlying language can be identified with a known language family.
The Phaistos Disc, found on Crete, uses a still different, stamped hieroglyphic-style script unrelated to Linear A in its known form.
An even earlier system, Cretan Hieroglyphic, was in use on the island before Linear A developed.

secondaryImage.caption: Agia Triada, site of one of the largest surviving Linear A archives.

milestones.text: Arthur Evans finds Linear A tablets at Knossos; the largest group later comes from Hagia Triada.
Louis Godart and Jean-Pierre Olivier publish GORILA, the standard corpus of the inscriptions. The script remains undeciphered.

summary: The script of Minoan Crete — readable in sound but not in meaning, because the language behind it is unknown.
significance: The writing of Minoan Crete, still undeciphered — and the script from which Linear B was adapted.
body:
Linear A is a syllabary of about 90 signs plus logograms for commodities and a decimal number system including fractions. It appears on clay tablets, sealings, and — unusually — on stone libation vessels and gold and silver objects, so it was used for religious dedication as well as everyday accounting. It was not even the first script on Crete: an earlier, still more poorly understood system now called Cretan Hieroglyphic was already in use before Linear A developed from it, and the famous Phaistos Disc, stamped rather than incised with a set of 45 repeating pictorial signs, represents yet another, wholly separate system whose signs do not match either script and whose authenticity and origin remain debated in their own right.

We can pronounce much of Linear A, in a rough phonetic sense. Linear B was adapted from Linear A to write Mycenaean Greek, so shared signs presumably kept broadly similar sound values, and applying those known Linear B values to Linear A texts produces plausible sound-sequences. But those sequences are not Greek, not any known Semitic language, and not convincingly anything else scholars have proposed. Around 1,400 documents survive, the great majority of them short administrative fragments from sites like Agia Triada in southern Crete, and that is far too small and repetitive a corpus for the kind of statistical decipherment that cracked other unknown scripts.

Proposals connecting the underlying language to Luwian and other Anatolian languages, to Etruscan, to Phoenician-related Semitic languages, and to several other candidates have all been argued at length and have all failed to convince a majority of specialists. Without either a genuine bilingual text pairing Linear A with a known language, or a substantially larger body of connected, non-formulaic writing, most epigraphers regard the language behind Linear A as likely to remain unread indefinitely.

name: Linear B

claims.text: Linear B records an early form of Greek.
It was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952.
All known Linear B texts are administrative records.
The script represents Greek phonology imperfectly.
Literacy in Linear B was confined to palace administrators.
Michael Ventris was a professionally trained architect and self-taught amateur, not an academic linguist, when he deciphered the script.
The American classicist Alice Kober's pre-war grid analysis of recurring sign patterns supplied essential groundwork that Ventris built directly on.

milestones.text: Arthur Evans finds thousands of tablets at Knossos.
Carl Blegen finds the Pylos archive, proving the script was used on the mainland.
Michael Ventris shows that the tablets record an early form of Greek.

summary: The earliest form of written Greek — a syllabary badly suited to the language, used only for palace accounting.
significance: The earliest written Greek, and the main source for how the Mycenaean palaces worked.
body:
Linear B writes Greek with a syllabary evidently designed first for some other, unrelated language, and the fit is genuinely poor. The script cannot distinguish *l* from *r*, has no consistent way to mark aspiration, and regularly drops final consonants, so a sign group transliterated *pa-te* could in principle represent either *patēr* (father) or *pantes* (all) — reading any given tablet requires constant contextual judgement rather than straightforward transcription, which is part of why the decipherment took as long as it did once scholars finally had enough tablets to work with.

Every one of the thousands of surviving tablets is a piece of palace administration, and nothing else. They record flocks and the shepherds responsible for them, wool quotas owed to the palace, allocations of bronze for smiths, chariot wheels specifically noted as serviceable or broken, rations issued to groups of women textile workers together with their children, and offerings to named gods including, on tablets from both Knossos and Pylos, an early form of Zeus. There is no literature, no history, no law code and no private correspondence anywhere in the corpus — the tablets are disposable annual accounts, most surviving only because the palace buildings that stored them burned, baking the unfired clay hard enough to last three thousand years by accident.

The decipherment itself, achieved in 1952, is one of the genuine intellectual triumphs of twentieth-century scholarship, and it was accomplished largely outside professional academia. Michael Ventris was a trained architect by profession, not a career linguist, who had been fascinated by the mystery of the undeciphered Aegean scripts since meeting Arthur Evans as a schoolboy in 1936, and who worked on the problem essentially as a private obsession alongside his day job. He built directly on painstaking earlier groundwork by the American classicist Alice Kober, who had died in 1950 without cracking the script herself but whose systematic grid analysis, tracking which signs regularly changed together in ways consistent with grammatical case endings, gave Ventris the structural scaffolding he needed. Working from a similar grid organising signs by probable shared consonants and vowels without assuming what any individual sign actually sounded like, Ventris noticed that testing a cluster of signs as probable Cretan place names produced coherent results only if the underlying language was Greek — a conclusion he found so unexpected, given the prevailing assumption that Linear B recorded some lost non-Greek Minoan language, that he initially argued against his own emerging result before the evidence became impossible to resist.

When the Mycenaean palaces that used it collapsed at the end of the Bronze Age, the script vanished with them almost without trace, and Greece would not be reliably literate again for several centuries, using an entirely different, alphabetic script borrowed from the Phoenicians. Linear B was never a language of literature, religion or law in its own right; it was a tool built for and by palace bureaucracy, and it had no life at all outside the palace walls that generated it.

name: The Greek alphabet
signs: 24 letters in the standard Ionic form

claims.text: The Greek alphabet was adapted from a Phoenician consonantal script.
Unused Phoenician consonant signs were reassigned as vowels.
Greek letter names are meaningless in Greek but meaningful in Semitic languages.
The Latin alphabet descends from a western Greek variant via Etruscan.
Athens adopted the Ionic alphabet officially in 403 BC.
The Dipylon oinochoe, inscribed c. 740 BC, is among the earliest known examples of Greek alphabetic writing.
Early Greek inscriptions could run right to left, left to right, or boustrophedon, alternating direction line by line.

milestones.text: The Dipylon Oinochoe, carrying one of the oldest alphabetic Greek inscriptions, is found in Athens.
Nestor's Cup, with one of the earliest Greek verse inscriptions, is found at Pithekoussai.

summary: The first writing system to represent both consonants and vowels — adapted from Phoenician by repurposing unneeded signs.
significance: The first full alphabet with vowels, ancestor of the Latin and Cyrillic scripts used today.
body:
Phoenician script recorded consonants only. That works for Semitic languages, where roots are consonantal and vowels are largely predictable from context, but it fails badly for Greek, where vowel quality carries essential grammatical and lexical distinctions a reader cannot simply infer.

The Greek solution was to take Phoenician letters for sounds Greek did not have — the glottal stop *aleph*, the pharyngeal *ayin*, *he*, *yod* — and reassign them as alpha, omicron, epsilon and iota. The letter names came along untranslated: *aleph* means "ox" and *beth* means "house" in Phoenician, and mean nothing at all in Greek. That mismatch is itself strong proof of the borrowing, since no one inventing a script from scratch names its own letters with foreign words for unrelated objects.

Among the earliest surviving examples of the new script are the Dipylon oinochoe, a small jug from an Athenian grave dated to around 740 BC and scratched with a line of hexameter verse about a dancing contest, and the roughly contemporary "Nestor's Cup" from Pithekoussai off the Italian coast, whose inscription jokingly invokes the far grander drinking cup of the Homeric hero Nestor. Early Greek writing had no fixed direction: inscriptions could run right to left in the Phoenician manner, left to right, or boustrophedon — literally "as the ox turns" while ploughing — alternating direction with every line, sometimes even mirroring each letter's orientation to match. Local city alphabets also varied for generations in which extra signs they kept or dropped, including now-obsolete letters like digamma, qoppa and san, until Athens formally adopted the Ionic 24-letter standard in 403 BC, a decision that gradually became the model followed everywhere else.

The result could represent any Greek word unambiguously and, unlike Linear B or Egyptian hieroglyphs before it, could be learned by a child in weeks rather than by a scribe over years of specialised training — a difference in accessibility that scholars increasingly credit with helping to seed the unusually broad, non-priestly literacy of later Greek society. The western, Euboean variant of the alphabet travelled to Italy through colonies like Cumae and became Etruscan, then Latin, and so, by a long chain of transmission from a Semitic script devised for entirely different languages, the alphabet used for most of the world's writing today.

name: Koine Greek
status: Ancestor of Byzantine and Modern Greek

claims.text: Koine Greek developed primarily from Attic with Ionic influence.
It became the administrative and commercial lingua franca of the Hellenistic world.
Greek inscriptions of Ashoka survive at Kandahar in Afghanistan.
The Septuagint and New Testament are written in Koine.
Greek remained dominant in the eastern Mediterranean under Roman rule.
Educated Romans were routinely expected to be bilingual in Greek and Latin, and Greek was widely used in Roman literature, philosophy and diplomacy.

summary: The simplified common Greek that spread with Alexander's conquests and became the lingua franca from Marseille to the Indus.
significance: The common Greek of the Hellenistic and Roman East, the language of the New Testament and of Byzantium.
body:
Koine — literally "common" — grew out of Attic Greek with significant Ionic influence, spreading rapidly through the ranks of Alexander's armies, drawn from many different Greek-speaking regions, and through the administrative machinery of the vast territory he conquered. In the process it simplified considerably from its Classical Attic ancestor: the old dual grammatical number, used for pairs of things, disappeared almost entirely; the subtle optative mood fell into steady decline; the dative case began eroding in everyday speech; and vocabulary standardised across regions that had previously spoken quite distinct local dialects.

It became the first genuine lingua franca of the Mediterranean and Near Eastern world. A merchant from Massalia in southern Gaul and a government official in Babylon could conduct business with one another in essentially the same language, something no earlier common tongue had achieved across so vast an area. Inscriptions in Koine turn up as far away as Afghanistan and northern India — the famous edicts of the Buddhist Indian emperor Ashoka at Kandahar were carved in both Greek and Aramaic, meaning a South Asian emperor addressed his own Greek-speaking subjects in the Greek language as a matter of practical necessity. It is also, crucially, the language of both the Septuagint, the Greek translation of Hebrew scripture undertaken in Alexandria, and later the entire New Testament, which is precisely why so much of the technical vocabulary of Hellenistic Greek administrative and philosophical culture ended up permanently embedded in the language of Christian theology.

Rome ultimately conquered the entire Greek-speaking world militarily and politically without ever managing, or even much attempting, to displace it linguistically. Educated Romans were routinely expected to be genuinely bilingual in Greek and Latin, Greek literature and philosophy were treated as the essential foundation of a proper Roman education, and Greek remained the practical working language of diplomacy, commerce and scholarship across the eastern Mediterranean for a further thousand years, well into the Byzantine period and long after the Western Roman Empire itself had fallen.

name: The Achaemenid Empire

claims.text: The Achaemenid Empire extended from the Aegean to the Indus at its greatest extent.
Darius I organised it into satrapies with fixed tribute obligations.
The Royal Road connected Sardis to Susa with relay stations.
Administrative tablets record rationed wages paid to male and female workers.
Greek accounts of Persia are systematically shaped by hostility.
The Cyrus Cylinder records Cyrus the Great permitting displaced peoples, including Judean exiles in Babylon, to return home and restore their own temples.
The elite infantry corps the Greeks called the "Immortals" was kept permanently at a strength of 10,000 by immediately replacing any casualty.

summary: The largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean to the Indus, and the defining external power in Greek history.
significance: The great empire that Greece fought in the Persian Wars and Alexander conquered, shaping Greek history for two centuries.
body:
Founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BC, the Achaemenid Empire eventually governed perhaps 25 million people — a substantial fraction of humanity alive at the time — across the Balkans, Egypt, Anatolia, Mesopotamia, Iran and Central Asia, making it by a wide margin the largest state the world had yet seen. Cyrus set the tone for how it would rule from the start: the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay proclamation issued after his conquest of Babylon, records him permitting displaced peoples, including Judean exiles held in Babylon, to return to their homelands and rebuild their own temples — a policy of restoring rather than erasing conquered peoples' institutions that some modern commentators have controversially compared to an early human-rights charter, and that in any case gave the empire's early conquests real practical legitimacy in the eyes of those it absorbed.

Its administrative achievement was genuine and durable. Darius I divided the empire into satrapies, each with a fixed tribute obligation and a Persian governor typically balanced by independent royal inspectors the Greeks called "the King's Eyes and Ears," standardised a gold coin called the daric, and built the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, its relay stations allowing couriers on the royal messenger system to cover roughly 2,700 kilometres in about a week — a speed of long-distance communication nothing else in the ancient Mediterranean world matched. Local languages, religions, legal codes and even local rulers were generally left in place under this system rather than replaced with Persian equivalents; the empire governed through administered diversity rather than enforced uniformity, an approach that let it hold together dozens of previously independent kingdoms and cultures for two centuries. Its military reflected the same scale: the elite infantry corps the Greeks called the "Immortals," after the Persian custom of instantly replacing any casualty so the unit's paper strength of 10,000 never visibly changed, became one of the most recognisable images of Persian power in Greek accounts of the wars between the two.

Those Greek accounts are, however, almost the entirety of what popular memory of Persia is actually built on, and they are systematically hostile, written by people with an obvious interest in explaining and dignifying a Greek military victory against overwhelming numerical odds. Persian administrative sources tell a considerably less lurid story: the Persepolis Fortification tablets, an enormous cache of everyday bureaucratic records rather than royal propaganda, show ordinary wages paid in grain, wine and other rations to workers of both sexes on the palace's own payroll, including specific extra rations recorded for women who had recently given birth — the routine texture of an administered state rather than the despotic caricature that dominates Herodotus and later Greek tradition.

Alexander the Great destroyed the empire's political independence in a single sustained campaign between 334 and 330 BC, defeating Darius III in three major battles and burning the ceremonial capital of Persepolis, but he then governed much of the conquered territory using the Achaemenid empire's own administrative machinery largely intact, retaining Persian satraps and Persian methods of taxation and communication rather than replacing them wholesale — an implicit acknowledgment that the system Cyrus and Darius had built worked well enough to be worth keeping, even for the man who had just destroyed the dynasty that built it.

name: The Ptolemaic Kingdom

claims.text: The Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt from 305 to 30 BC.
The Ptolemies presented themselves as pharaohs to Egyptians and Greek kings to Greeks.
Key commodities including grain, oil and papyrus were royal monopolies.
The dynasty practised sibling marriage.
Fourteen successive Ptolemaic kings were all named Ptolemy, distinguished today mainly by modern numbering and epithets.
Ptolemy VIII's reign was marked by exceptionally violent family purges, including the killing and dismemberment of his own son by his first wife.

summary: Greek-ruled Egypt under Alexander's general Ptolemy and his descendants — the wealthiest and longest-lasting successor kingdom.
significance: The richest of the Hellenistic kingdoms, home of the Library of Alexandria, and the last to fall to Rome.
body:
The Ptolemies governed Egypt for 275 years as a Greek-speaking elite over an Egyptian population, presenting themselves as pharaohs to Egyptians and as Hellenistic kings to Greeks. Temple reliefs show them in pharaonic dress making offerings to Egyptian gods; their coins show them in Greek royal diadems.

The economy was tightly controlled. Grain, oil and papyrus were state monopolies, and Egypt's agricultural surplus made the kingdom enormously rich — wealth that funded the Library, the Museum and the Pharos.

The dynasty practised sibling marriage, following Egyptian royal precedent, which produced a genealogy of extraordinary complexity and a great deal of murder within the family. Fourteen kings in direct succession were all named Ptolemy, distinguished today only by modern numbering and by epithets ancient writers or later historians attached to them — Ptolemy III "Euergetes," the Benefactor, against Ptolemy VIII "Physcon," the Fatty, whose own reign is remembered as one of the family's most violently self-destructive: he had his ten-year-old son by his first wife, Cleopatra II, killed and dismembered, and reportedly sent the pieces to her as a birthday gift, in the course of a decades-long civil war between rival branches of the same family for the throne.

Cleopatra VII was the dynasty's last ruler, and by most accounts one of its most capable, holding Egypt's independence together through alliances first with Julius Caesar and then with Mark Antony against the growing power of Rome. Her and Antony's defeat at the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC, followed by both their deaths the following year as the victorious Octavian's forces closed in on Alexandria, ended Ptolemaic Egypt after two hundred and seventy-five years and, with it, brought the entire Hellenistic age to a formal close — the last of Alexander's successor kingdoms finally absorbed into what would shortly become the Roman Empire.

name: The Seleucid Empire

claims.text: The Seleucid Empire was the largest of Alexander's successor states.
The Seleucid Era, beginning 312/311 BC, was the first continuous numbered year-count.
The Seleucids founded numerous Greek cities across Asia as instruments of control.
The empire lost its eastern provinces progressively to Parthia and Bactria.
Antiochus IV's attempt to impose Greek religious practice in Jerusalem provoked the Maccabean revolt.
Rome's victory at Magnesia in 190 BC forced the Seleucids to abandon their territory in Anatolia.

summary: The largest successor state, inheriting most of Alexander's Asian conquests from Anatolia to Central Asia.
significance: The largest of the Hellenistic kingdoms, which spread Greek cities and culture from Syria to Central Asia.
body:
Seleucus I took Babylonia in 312 BC — the year from which the Seleucid Era counts, making it the first continuous numbered year-count in recorded history and, through a long chain of borrowed conventions, an ancestor of the AD dating system still used worldwide.

The empire's fundamental problem was its own enormous size and diversity. It governed Greeks, Babylonians, Persians, Jews, Bactrians and dozens of other peoples spread across a territory stretching from the Aegean to the borders of India, and held them together primarily by founding dozens of new Greek cities as anchors of military and administrative control — Antioch, Seleucia-on-the-Tigris, Apamea, Laodicea and many more, each populated with Greek and Macedonian settlers loyal to the crown in regions that otherwise had little natural attachment to it.

It lost territory steadily rather than all at once: the far eastern provinces first to the Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta, then further territory to the nomadic Parthians, who eventually took Mesopotamia itself; Bactria broke away entirely as an independent Greek kingdom; and Anatolia was lost outright to Rome after the decisive defeat at Magnesia in 190 BC, a battle that forced the Seleucids to abandon essentially all their territory west of the Taurus mountains under the harsh terms of the subsequent Treaty of Apamea. Domestically, Antiochus IV's aggressive attempt to impose Greek religious practice on the Temple in Jerusalem, including reportedly erecting an altar to Zeus within it, provoked the Maccabean revolt, a Jewish uprising that eventually won effective independence for Judaea.

Pompey annexed what little remained of the once-vast empire as a Roman province in 63 BC, ending it after nearly two and a half centuries of slow, uneven contraction from its original scale.

name: Crete

claims.text: Crete was settled by farming populations arriving by sea around 7000 BC.
It hosted Europe's first palace-based state society.
Its position linked Aegean, Egyptian and Levantine trade routes.
Crete's mountainous interior sustained isolated highland communities and dialects even after Bronze Age palatial society collapsed.

summary: The largest Greek island, home of Europe's first palace civilisation and a crossroads between the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant.
significance: Home of the Minoans, Europe's first palace civilisation, and a crossroads between the Aegean, Egypt and the Near East.
body:
Crete is 260 km long, mountainous, and positioned where the sea routes from Egypt, the Levant and the Aegean converge. That position explains most of its history.

It was settled by around 7000 BC by farmers who brought livestock and crops by boat — one of the earliest maritime colonisations known. The palaces emerged around 1900 BC and dominated the Aegean until the destructions of 1450 BC.

After the Bronze Age it became comparatively marginal: a land of many small, frequently feuding poleis, known for skilled archers, mercenaries hired out across the wider Greek world, and, in the standard Greek stereotype, a reputation for lying. The "Cretan paradox" — a Cretan saying all Cretans are liars — enters logic as a foundational puzzle about self-reference and eventually turns up quoted in the New Testament's Epistle to Titus. The island's rugged, mountainous interior sustained isolated highland communities with their own dialects and customs well after Bronze Age palatial society had collapsed elsewhere on the island, a fragmentation that persisted through the Archaic and Classical periods even as the rest of the Aegean world consolidated into more familiar, better-known city-states.

Rome took the island in 69–67 BC after a difficult campaign against determined local resistance.

name: The Cyclades

claims.text: Melian obsidian was traded across the Aegean from the Mesolithic onwards.
Parian and Naxian marble supplied Greek sculpture throughout antiquity.
Early Cycladic culture produced distinctive marble figurines c. 3200–2000 BC.
Cycladic figurines strongly influenced early twentieth-century modernist sculptors including Brancusi and Henry Moore.
Delos was ritually purified by Athens, which removed existing graves from the island to preserve its sanctity.

summary: The ring of Aegean islands around Delos — source of marble, obsidian and the earliest distinctive art of the Aegean.
significance: The islands where the first distinctive Aegean art appeared, and home of the sacred island of Delos.
body:
The name means "the circle", from the islands ringing sacred Delos, which both Athens and other Greek states treated as neutral ground holy enough to require ritual purification: Athens at one point had every existing grave on Delos dug up and the remains relocated to a neighbouring island, so that no death would be permitted to pollute the sanctuary going forward. The islands themselves are small, dry, and individually poor in farmland, which made their inhabitants exceptional sailors out of sheer necessity: almost everything of value had to move between islands, and beyond them, by sea.

Their mineral and stone resources mattered far beyond their modest size. Melos supplied volcanic obsidian traded across the wider Aegean from as early as the Mesolithic period, long before farming or metalworking arrived in the region at all. Paros and Naxos supplied the fine white marble used first for the distinctive Cycladic figurines and later for some of the finest sculpture in the entire Greek tradition — the Nike of Samothrace and the Venus de Milo are both carved from Parian marble.

The Early Cycladic culture of roughly 3200 to 2000 BC produced the austere, folded-arm marble figurines now found in museums worldwide, along with the mysterious engraved "frying pans" whose exact purpose remains debated, and maintained trade networks that the later, more famous Minoan and Mycenaean palace civilisations essentially inherited wholesale. Those spare, geometric figurines, largely ignored by scholars as primitive curiosities for much of the modern era, went on to influence early twentieth-century sculptors including Constantin Brancusi and Henry Moore, whose own pared-down forms often echo Cycladic simplicity directly.

Thera, at the southern edge of the group, erupted catastrophically around 1600 BC in one of the largest volcanic events of the ancient world, burying the settlement at Akrotiri and reshaping the whole island into its present crescent form.

name: Cyprus

claims.text: Cypriot copper was mined and exported across the Mediterranean from the Bronze Age.
The Latin cuprum ("copper") derives from the island's name.
Cyprus was divided among roughly ten city-kingdoms with mixed Greek and Phoenician populations through the Archaic and Classical periods.
Cyprus returned to stable Ptolemaic control by the 290s BC and remained so until 58 BC.
Cyprus was restored to Ptolemaic rule from 48 to 30 BC after its first Roman annexation.
Cyprus developed its own syllabic script, distinct from both Linear B and the alphabet, used to write Greek and an unrelated local language.
Paphos, on Cyprus, was one of the principal cult centres of Aphrodite, whose myth held that she was born from the sea nearby.

summary: A copper-rich island facing the Levant, divided among small Greek–Phoenician city-kingdoms and later secured as one of the Ptolemies' most valuable possessions.
significance: A crossroads of Greek and Near Eastern culture, rich in copper, and the legendary birthplace of Aphrodite.
body:
Cyprus sits close enough to the Levantine coast to trade with it constantly and far enough offshore to develop on its own terms. Its copper mines supplied the Bronze Age Mediterranean on a scale that shaped the island's whole economy and external relationships; the Latin word for the metal, *cuprum*, derives from the island's own name rather than the other way round, a linguistic trace of just how closely the two were associated in the ancient world.

Through the Archaic and Classical periods it was never one state but around ten small city-kingdoms — Salamis, Paphos, Kition, Kourion and others — with mixed Greek and Phoenician populations, nominally subject in turn to Assyria, then Egypt, then Persia, while their own kings struck their own coins and fought each other as readily as any outside power. That persistent fragmentation made the island a strategic prize repeatedly fought over rather than a unified power projecting force of its own. Cypriot scribes developed a distinctive syllabic script of their own, unrelated in form to the Linear scripts of Crete and Greece or to the alphabet, and used it to write both Greek and an unrelated, still poorly understood local Eteocypriot language side by side for centuries, a linguistic layering that has made bilingual Cypriot inscriptions valuable evidence for scholars working on both languages. Paphos, on the island's southwest coast, was one of the most important cult centres of Aphrodite anywhere in the Greek world, tradition holding that the goddess had risen from the sea foam just offshore.

After Alexander's death it was fought over repeatedly by his successors. Demetrius Poliorcetes broke Ptolemaic control of the island at the naval battle of Salamis in 306 BC, but Ptolemy I recovered it by the 290s BC, and his dynasty held it as a core possession — a naval base and a steady supply of copper and timber — for over two centuries. Rome annexed Cyprus outright in 58 BC in a controversial seizure orchestrated partly by Cato the Younger; Ptolemaic rule was briefly restored from 48 to 30 BC, largely at Julius Caesar's and then Mark Antony's initiative, before the island returned permanently to direct Roman control after Actium.

name: The Hittite Empire

claims.text: Hittite archives refer to a power called Ahhiyawa across the sea.
They name a city Wilusa in north-west Anatolia and a king Alaksandu.
Hattusa was destroyed and abandoned around 1190 BC.
Ahhiyawa refers to Mycenaean Greeks.
Wilusa is Homeric Ilios and Alaksandu is connected to Alexandros/Paris.
The Hittite state was a genuine great power, corresponding as an equal with Egypt, Babylon, and Assyria in a documented international diplomatic system.

summary: The Anatolian great power whose archives name Mycenaean Greeks — and whose collapse is the clearest marker of the Bronze Age crisis.
significance: The great Anatolian power whose records mention the Mycenaean Greeks and Troy, and whose fall marks the Bronze Age collapse.
body:
The Hittites ruled central Anatolia from Hattusa and fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh around 1274 BC, producing the earliest surviving peace treaty, of which both Egyptian and Hittite copies exist.

Hatti stood as one of a small handful of recognised great powers in the Late Bronze Age Near East, exchanging royal letters, treaties and diplomatic marriages on equal terms with Egypt, Babylon and Assyria — a documented international system of the kind the Aegean world outside Hittite records leaves almost no direct trace of, which is exactly why the Ahhiyawa references below matter so much to reconstructing the Mycenaean Greeks' place in that wider world.

For Greek history their archives are decisive. They record a land called Ahhiyawa across the sea, whose king is treated at times as a great king and equal — generally identified with a Mycenaean Greek power. They also name Wilusa, plausibly Homeric *(W)ilios*, and a king of Wilusa called Alaksandu, which sits uncomfortably close to Alexandros, the alternative name of Paris.

This is the only external written evidence for the Mycenaean world, and it comes from an empire that Greek tradition entirely forgot.

That empire did not long outlast the Bronze Age world it helped illuminate: Hattusa itself was burned and abandoned around 1190 BC, within the same general wave of destructions — from Mycenaean palaces to Ugarit to, on one reading, Troy VIIa — now known as the Bronze Age Collapse.

name: The polis

claims.text: Greece in the Classical period contained over a thousand separate poleis.
Most poleis were small, with a few thousand citizens or fewer.
The polis took shape as a political community during the 8th century BC.
Aristotle defined the human being as a creature whose nature is to live in a polis.

summary: The Greek city-state: a self-governing community of citizens with its town, its territory and its gods — the basic unit of Greek political life.
significance: Almost everything distinctively Greek — citizenship, democracy, political philosophy, the hoplite army — grew within the polis, and the word lives on in "politics".
body:
A polis was a self-governing community of citizens: a town, usually with an acropolis and an agora (public square), together with the farmland around it. It took shape across the Greek world during the 8th century BC, the same period that saw the first monumental temples, the alphabet and the spread of colonies. By the Classical period there were well over a thousand poleis, from the Black Sea to Spain.

Most were small. A typical polis had a few hundred to a few thousand adult male citizens; Athens and Sparta, with tens of thousands, were exceptional. Each had its own laws, magistrates, coinage, calendar, army and patron gods, and fiercely guarded its independence (*autonomia*). Government ranged from kingship and narrow oligarchy to the democracy of Athens, but in nearly all, citizens shared in decisions through assemblies and councils.

The polis defined identity. Citizenship was usually inherited and jealously limited; women, slaves and resident foreigners lived in the city without full membership. Citizens fought for it as hoplites or rowers, and worshipped its gods together at its festivals. Aristotle called the human being a "political animal" — a creature made to live in a polis.

The independence of the poleis was also their weakness: they fought each other constantly. After Philip II and Alexander, real power passed to kings and then to Rome, though the polis survived as the framework of city life across the Hellenistic East.

name: Athenian democracy

claims.text: Athenian democracy was direct: citizens voted in person in the Assembly rather than electing representatives.
Most magistrates and all jurors were chosen by lot.
Political rights were restricted to adult male citizens, perhaps 30,000 in the 4th century BC.
Pay for public service was introduced under Pericles to let poorer citizens take part.
The democracy was abolished by Macedonian intervention in 322 BC.

summary: The system by which the citizens of Athens governed themselves directly, through an open Assembly, a Council chosen by lot and mass citizen juries, from 508 to 322 BC.
significance: The first well-documented democracy in history, and the model — admired and criticised — behind every later idea of government by the people.
body:
Athenian democracy (*dēmokratia*, "power of the people") was created by Cleisthenes' reforms of 508/7 BC, building on Solon's earlier changes, and deepened in the 460s and 450s BC by Ephialtes and Pericles. It lasted, with two brief oligarchic interruptions in 411 and 404 BC, until Macedon abolished it in 322 BC.

It was direct democracy. The Assembly (*ekklēsia*), open to every adult male citizen, met about forty times a year on the Pnyx hill and voted on war, peace, laws and finance; any citizen could speak. A Council of 500, chosen each year by lot from the ten tribes, prepared its business. Most officials were also chosen by lot for one year, on the principle that ordinary citizens could govern; only military generals and some financial officers were elected. Mass juries of hundreds of citizens, also chosen by lot, decided cases in the law courts, and ostracism could exile a dangerously powerful man. From the 450s citizens were paid for jury service and later for attending the Assembly, so the poor could take part.

Its limits were sharp. Only free adult men of citizen birth — perhaps 30,000 in the 4th century BC — had political rights. Women, resident foreigners and a large enslaved population were excluded, and the democracy ruled an empire of subject allies.

Ancient critics such as Plato thought it rule by the ignorant mob; its defenders, like Pericles in Thucydides, saw it as the source of Athens' greatness.

name: Greek tyranny

claims.text: Tyranny in Archaic Greece meant one-man rule seized outside the traditional constitution, not necessarily cruel rule.
Cypselus of Corinth, around 657 BC, is among the earliest known tyrants.
Tyrants often weakened aristocratic power and sponsored public building and festivals.
Few tyrannies lasted beyond the second generation.

summary: One-man rule seized outside the traditional constitution, common across the Greek cities in the 7th and 6th centuries BC and later in Sicily.
significance: A stage through which many Greek cities passed on the way from aristocratic rule to broader citizen government — and the origin of the word "tyrant".
body:
A *tyrannos* was a ruler who took sole power outside the city's traditional constitution, usually by force or popular support. The word was not originally an insult: many tyrants governed effectively and were remembered with some gratitude. Only later, especially in democratic Athens, did "tyrant" come to mean a cruel and lawless despot.

Tyranny spread through the Greek cities from the mid-7th century BC, when growing wealth, colonisation and the rise of hoplite armies strained the power of the old aristocracies. Among the first was Cypselus of Corinth, around 657 BC; others included Pheidon of Argos, Polycrates of Samos, Cleisthenes of Sicyon and Peisistratus of Athens. Many tyrants weakened rival noble families, sponsored temples, harbours, aqueducts and festivals, and attracted poets and artists to their courts.

Few tyrannies outlasted a second generation. Their sons were often harsher and less able, and were overthrown — as Hippias was at Athens in 510 BC, with Spartan help. The fall of tyranny opened the way, in some cities, to democracy.

In Sicily, where war with Carthage favoured strong leaders, tyranny lasted much longer: Gelon and Hieron at Syracuse in the 5th century BC, Dionysius I in the 4th, and Agathocles at its end. Greek political thinkers from Herodotus to Plato and Aristotle treated tyranny as the worst of constitutions.

name: Hoplites and the phalanx

claims.text: Hoplites were heavy infantry named after their large round shield (hoplon or aspis).
A hoplite usually provided his own equipment, which tied military service to property.
The Chigi Vase of c. 650 BC is among the earliest images of hoplites in formation.
The phalanx developed gradually rather than through a single 7th-century "hoplite reform".

summary: The heavily armed citizen infantry of the Greek city-states, fighting shoulder to shoulder in the close formation called the phalanx.
significance: The way of fighting that defined Greek warfare for three centuries — and tied military duty, and political rights, to the citizen who could afford his own armour.
body:
A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier, named after his equipment (*hopla*) and above all his large round shield, the *aspis*, about a metre across, held on the left arm. He also wore a bronze helmet, a breastplate of bronze or linen, and greaves, and fought with a thrusting spear about 2.5 m long and a short sword. The full set was expensive, and hoplites usually bought their own, so they came from the middling and wealthier farmers of each city.

Hoplites fought in the phalanx, a formation usually eight ranks deep in which each man's shield partly covered the man to his left. Battles between phalanxes were short and brutal: the lines met, pushed and stabbed until one side broke and ran. Images such as the Chigi Vase of around 650 BC show the formation already in use, though whether it appeared suddenly in a "hoplite reform" or developed gradually is debated.

Because the city's defence rested on its hoplites, many historians link their rise to the decline of aristocratic rule and the spread of broader citizen government. Sparta made hoplite fighting a professional way of life and was long thought invincible, until Epaminondas broke its phalanx at Leuctra in 371 BC.

Hoplites beat Persian infantry at Marathon and Plataea, but from the 4th century BC they were overtaken by light troops, mercenaries and finally the Macedonian pike phalanx armed with the sarissa.

name: The trireme

claims.text: A trireme was rowed by about 170 oarsmen arranged in three levels.
Triremes fought mainly by ramming with a bronze ram at the bow.
Athenian rowers were mostly poorer citizens (thetes), along with metics and slaves.
The full-scale reconstruction Olympias, launched in 1987, reached speeds of about 9 knots.

summary: The fast, oared warship with three banks of rowers that dominated Greek naval warfare from the late 6th century BC.
significance: The ship that won Salamis, built Athens' empire and gave its poorest citizens, who rowed it, a decisive voice in the democracy.
body:
The trireme (*triērēs*) was a long, narrow warship about 37 m long and 5 m wide, rowed by around 170 men sitting in three levels on each side, with a small crew of officers, sailors, archers and marines — about 200 men in all. It carried sails for cruising but was rowed in battle. At its bow was a bronze ram at the waterline, the ship's main weapon: triremes fought by driving into the side or oars of an enemy ship. Skilled crews could also sweep past an enemy to shear off its oars.

The type spread through the Greek and Phoenician world in the later 6th century BC. In 483 BC Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend a windfall of silver on some 200 triremes, and in 480 BC that fleet won the battle of Salamis in the narrow straits off Attica. Afterwards the fleet became the instrument of Athenian power, policing the Delian League and keeping grain flowing from the Black Sea.

Rowing a trireme took training but not wealth, so the rowers of Athens were mostly its poorer citizens, the *thetes*, along with resident foreigners and some slaves. Ancient writers linked their importance in war to their power in the democratic Assembly.

A full-size reconstruction, the *Olympias*, built by the Hellenic Navy and launched in 1987, showed that such a ship could reach about 9 knots under oar. Its original was lost when Athens' last fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami in 405 BC.

name: Slavery in ancient Greece

claims.text: Chattel slavery was widespread in Greek cities, and slaves could be bought, sold and owned as property.
Classical Athens had a large enslaved population, perhaps 60,000–80,000, though estimates vary widely.
Spartan helots were a subject population bound to the land rather than individually owned chattel slaves.
Aristotle argued that some people were slaves by nature.

summary: The ownership and forced labour of human beings, built into the economy and society of nearly every Greek city.
significance: The hidden foundation of Greek civilisation: the leisure of citizens, the silver of Athens and the farms of Sparta all rested on unfree labour.
body:
Slavery existed throughout Greek history, from the palace workers recorded on Linear B tablets to the households of the Hellenistic kingdoms. In most cities it took the form of chattel slavery: slaves were property who could be bought, sold, punished and freed by their owners. They came mainly from war captives, piracy and the slave trade with peoples beyond the Greek world, such as Thracians and Scythians; Greeks enslaved other Greeks after wars, as Athens did at Melos.

In Classical Athens slaves worked in households, workshops and farms, as public servants and police, and in brutal conditions in the silver mines of Laurion. Estimates of their numbers vary, perhaps 60,000 to 80,000 in Attica at its height. Some skilled slaves lived and worked independently and could save to buy their freedom.

Sparta was different. Its helots, mainly the conquered people of Messenia, were not owned by individuals but bound to the land as a subject population, farming it for Spartan citizens. They far outnumbered their masters, and Sparta held them down by violence; their liberation in 369 BC ended Spartan power.

Few Greeks questioned slavery itself. Aristotle argued that some people were slaves by nature; a few Sophists and later Stoics suggested that slavery was a matter of law, not nature. Modern historians stress that Greek freedom and democracy for citizens existed alongside, and depended on, the unfreedom of others.

name: Women in ancient Greece

claims.text: Athenian citizen women had no political rights and were legally under the guardianship of a male relative.
Spartan women could own and inherit property and exercised in public.
Women held important public roles in religion, as priestesses and in festivals.
Hellenistic queens such as Arsinoe II and Cleopatra VII exercised real political power.

summary: The lives, roles and restrictions of women in the Greek world, which varied greatly between cities and periods.
significance: Half of the population, largely missing from political history, yet central to religion, the household and much of Greek literature.
body:
Most of what survives about Greek women was written by men, and most of it concerns Athens, where their position was especially restricted. An Athenian citizen woman could not vote, hold office or own significant property in her own name, and was legally under the guardianship (*kyrieia*) of her father, husband or nearest male relative. Girls married young, often at fourteen or fifteen, to husbands chosen for them, and respectable women were expected to manage the household (*oikos*) and stay largely out of public view. Poorer women, however, worked in markets, fields and crafts.

Religion was the great exception. Women served as priestesses — the priestess of Athena Polias at Athens and the Pythia at Delphi were among the most important religious figures in Greece — and took part in festivals, some of them, such as the Thesmophoria, for women only.

Elsewhere things differed. Spartan women owned and inherited land, exercised in public and were known for speaking their minds. Some women became famous in their own right: the poet Sappho on Lesbos, Aspasia of Miletus in Athens, the philosopher Hipparchia, and Cynisca of Sparta, the first woman to win at Olympia.

In the Hellenistic kingdoms royal women such as Olympias, Arsinoe II and Cleopatra VII wielded real political power. Greek drama, from Antigone to Medea, repeatedly put women's voices and conflicts at its centre.

name: Greek religion

claims.text: Greek religion had no single sacred book, creed or professional priestly caste.
Animal sacrifice followed by a shared feast was the central ritual act.
Several Olympian gods, including Zeus, Hera and Poseidon, are named on Linear B tablets.
Each polis had its own patron deities, festivals and calendar.

summary: The beliefs and rituals through which Greeks honoured their many gods — a religion of practice, festivals and sacrifice rather than doctrine.
significance: Religion ran through every part of Greek life, from household and city to theatre, athletics and war; its gods and myths remain the best-known legacy of ancient Greece.
body:
Greek religion had no founder, no holy book, no creed and no church. It was a matter of practice: honouring the gods in the right way so that they would favour the community. Its roots reach back to the Bronze Age — Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus are already named on Linear B tablets — and its stories were given lasting shape by Homer and Hesiod.

The Greeks worshipped many gods. The twelve Olympians — Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and Hestia or Dionysus — were joined by countless local gods, nymphs and heroes. Each city had its own patron deities and calendar of festivals, such as the Panathenaia at Athens.

The central ritual was animal sacrifice at an outdoor altar, followed by a shared meal of the meat, which bound the community to its gods and to each other. People also offered prayers, libations, first fruits and dedications, from cheap figurines to marble statues and whole treasuries. Temples were houses for the gods' images, not places of congregation. Priests and priestesses served particular cults, often as a civic office.

Greeks sought the gods' guidance through oracles, above all at Delphi and Dodona, and through omens. Panhellenic sanctuaries such as Olympia and Delphi brought the scattered Greek cities together. For many, mystery cults such as those of Eleusis offered a more personal hope for the afterlife.

Greek religion slowly gave way to Christianity and was banned under Theodosius I in the AD 390s.

name: The Panhellenic Games
altNames: Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean Games

claims.text: The four Panhellenic festivals were held at Olympia, Delphi, the Isthmus of Corinth and Nemea.
Victors at the Panhellenic games received only a wreath, but were richly honoured by their home cities.
The traditional date of the first Olympic Games is 776 BC.
The Olympic Games ended under Theodosius I around AD 393.

summary: The four great athletic and religious festivals open to all Greeks — the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean Games.
significance: The Games brought rival cities together under a shared truce, gave Greece a common calendar and created the ideal of athletic excellence that the modern Olympics revived.
body:
Four festivals formed the "circuit" (*periodos*) of games open to Greeks from every city. The Olympic Games, for Zeus at Olympia, were held every four years from, by tradition, 776 BC. The Pythian Games, for Apollo at Delphi, were held every four years from 586 BC and included music and poetry contests. The Isthmian Games, for Poseidon near Corinth, and the Nemean Games, for Zeus at Nemea, were held every two years. Their prizes were simple wreaths — olive, laurel, pine and celery.

The festivals were religious occasions, with sacrifices and processions as well as competition. Events included foot races, the pentathlon, wrestling, boxing and the brutal *pankration*, and chariot and horse races. Competitors were free Greek men, who competed naked. Women were barred from competing, though they could win the chariot races as owners of the horses, as the Spartan princess Cynisca did.

Although the prize was only a wreath, victory brought fame and reward at home: statues, free meals for life, and victory odes by poets such as Pindar. A sacred truce let athletes and spectators travel safely to the games, even through cities at war. Counting years by Olympiads gave the Greeks a shared way of dating events.

The Olympic Games continued under Roman rule until they were ended around AD 393. They were revived as the modern Olympic Games in Athens in 1896.

name: Greek theatre

claims.text: Tragedy and comedy were performed in competitions at Athenian festivals of Dionysus.
Thespis is traditionally credited with the first tragedy at the City Dionysia around 534 BC.
All actors were men, wearing masks and playing several roles each.
Only 32 or 33 complete tragedies and 11 comedies of Aristophanes survive from 5th-century Athens.

summary: The tragedy and comedy created in Athens for the festivals of Dionysus, performed by masked actors and a chorus in open-air theatres.
significance: The beginning of Western drama: the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes are still performed, and their forms underlie theatre to this day.
body:
Greek drama grew out of the worship of Dionysus at Athens. At the City Dionysia each spring, and at the smaller Lenaia, playwrights competed before audiences of thousands seated on the slope below the Acropolis. By tradition, Thespis staged the first tragedy around 534 BC; comedy was added to the festival in 486 BC.

A tragedy combined spoken scenes between actors with songs and dances by a chorus of twelve or fifteen. All performers were male citizens wearing masks, and two or three actors played all the speaking parts. Each tragic poet presented three tragedies and a comic satyr play. Wealthy citizens paid for the choruses as a public duty. Tragedies drew on myth — the families of Agamemnon and Oedipus, the Trojan War — to explore justice, fate, the gods and the conflicts of the city. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides are the only tragedians whose plays survive complete, about 32 in all.

Comedy was very different. The Old Comedy of Aristophanes mocked living politicians, philosophers and poets by name, with fantastic plots, obscene jokes and sharp political satire. By the late 4th century it had given way to the New Comedy of Menander, gentle plays of everyday family life and romance that shaped Roman comedy and, through it, later European drama.

Stone theatres, such as those at Athens and Epidaurus, spread across the Greek world. Aristotle's *Poetics* remains the first great analysis of drama.

name: The symposium

claims.text: The symposium was an all-male drinking party held in the men's room (andron) of a private house.
Wine was mixed with water in a krater, and drinking it unmixed was considered barbaric.
Much Archaic lyric poetry was composed for performance at symposia.
Many of the finest Athenian painted vases were made for use at the symposium.

summary: The Greek drinking party: an evening of wine, poetry, music, games and conversation among male citizens reclining on couches.
significance: The setting for much of Greek poetry, philosophy and vase painting — and a key institution of aristocratic and citizen social life.
body:
A symposium (*symposion*, "drinking together") was an evening gathering of men in the *andrōn*, the men's dining room of a private house, usually with seven to fifteen couches arranged around the walls. After dinner the guests reclined, garlanded, while a host or elected "symposiarch" decided how strong the wine should be. Greek wine was always mixed with water in a large bowl, the *kratēr*; drinking it neat was thought the habit of barbarians.

The evening followed rituals: libations to the gods, songs, toasts, riddles and games such as *kottabos*, flicking wine dregs at a target. Guests took turns singing or reciting, and much Archaic lyric poetry — by Alcaeus, Anacreon, Theognis and others — was composed for these occasions. Hired musicians, dancers and *hetairai* (educated female companions) might entertain; respectable citizen women did not attend.

The symposium was also a place of friendship, politics and love between men, where political factions formed and young men learned the values of their class. Plato's *Symposium* and Xenophon's dialogue of the same name portray philosophical conversation at such parties.

The symposium shaped Greek art. Many of the finest Athenian painted vessels — mixing bowls, wine jugs and drinking cups — were made for it, and they often show symposium scenes, as does the painted Tomb of the Diver at Paestum. Exported to Etruria, such vessels spread the custom of the banquet across the Mediterranean.

name: Education and the gymnasium

claims.text: Athenian education was private and paid for by families, covering letters, music and physical training.
Sparta was unusual in providing a compulsory state upbringing, the agoge, for citizen boys.
Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum were founded in or beside public gymnasia.
In the Hellenistic period the gymnasium became the centre of Greek civic and cultural identity in new cities across the East.

summary: How Greek boys — and occasionally girls — were brought up and taught, from the reading teacher and the wrestling school to the gymnasium and the philosophical schools.
significance: The Greek ideal of education (paideia) — a balance of mind and body, letters and music — became the foundation of education in the Roman world and, through it, Europe.
body:
In most Greek cities education was a private matter for families who could afford it. In Classical Athens a boy from a well-off family went from about seven to a *grammatistēs*, who taught reading, writing and arithmetic and made him learn Homer by heart; to a *kitharistēs*, who taught the lyre and lyric poetry; and to a *paidotribēs*, who trained him in wrestling, running and other sports at a wrestling ground (*palaistra*). A slave called a *paidagōgos* escorted him. Girls were usually taught at home, mainly household skills.

Sparta was the great exception: from about seven, citizen boys entered the *agoge*, a harsh state training in obedience, endurance and fighting. Spartan girls also exercised in public.

For older youths and men the centre of education was the *gymnasion*, a public exercise ground with tracks, baths and colonnades, which became a place for conversation and teaching. Socrates questioned young men there, and the Sophists offered paid courses in rhetoric. Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum were founded at Athenian gymnasia, and grew into the first lasting schools of higher learning. From the late 4th century, Athens trained its young men as *ephebes* for two years of military service.

In the Hellenistic world the gymnasium became the symbol of Greek life. New cities from Egypt to Afghanistan — Ai-Khanoum among them — built gymnasia, where Greek-speaking youths were trained in Greek letters and athletics.

name: Greek architecture

claims.text: The Doric and Ionic orders were established in stone by the 6th century BC.
Greek temples were built of carefully fitted blocks without mortar, joined by metal clamps.
Greek temples and their sculpture were originally brightly painted.
The Corinthian capital is first known from the temple of Apollo at Bassae, in the late 5th century BC.

summary: The temples, theatres, stoas and cities of the Greeks, built in the Doric, Ionic and later Corinthian orders.
significance: Greek temple design — columns, entablature and pediment, built on rules of proportion — became the basis of classical architecture from Rome to the present.
body:
Monumental Greek architecture began in the 7th century BC, when temples built of mud brick and timber started to be rebuilt in stone. The basic form was the temple: a rectangular room (*cella*) housing the god's statue, often surrounded by a colonnade and topped by a pitched roof with triangular pediments at each end. Temples faced east, towards an altar outside, where sacrifices were made.

Two systems, or orders, developed in the 6th century BC. The Doric order, used mainly on the mainland and in the west, has sturdy fluted columns with plain cushion capitals and no base, and a frieze of alternating triglyphs and metopes. The Ionic order, from the islands and Ionia, has slenderer columns on moulded bases, with scroll-shaped capitals and a continuous frieze. The Corinthian order, with capitals of acanthus leaves, first appears at Bassae in the late 5th century BC and became popular in the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

Builders fitted stone blocks precisely without mortar, using metal clamps, and refined their designs with subtle curves, as in the Parthenon. Buildings and their sculptures were brightly painted.

Beyond temples, Greeks built theatres, stoas (long colonnaded halls), council houses, gymnasia, fountain houses and fortifications. From the 5th century BC new cities were often laid out on regular grids, a practice associated with Hippodamus of Miletus. The Romans adopted Greek forms wholesale, and through them Greek architecture shaped European building for two thousand years.

name: Greek vase painting

claims.text: Athenian black-figure painting developed in the 7th century BC and dominated until about 530 BC.
Red-figure painting was invented in Athens around 530 BC.
Many painters and potters signed their work, allowing individual hands to be identified.
Large numbers of Athenian vases were exported to Etruria and found in Etruscan tombs.

summary: The painted pottery of ancient Greece, from abstract Geometric patterns to the black-figure and red-figure scenes of myth and daily life.
significance: The best-surviving Greek pictorial art: thousands of painted vessels preserve images of myth, ritual, war, sport and daily life that would otherwise be lost.
body:
Pottery survives far better than painting on walls or wood, so painted vases are the main record of Greek pictorial art. Fine pottery was made in many places, but Corinth and above all Athens led production.

After the Bronze Age, Protogeometric pottery (c. 1050–900 BC) and then Geometric pottery (c. 900–700 BC) were decorated with circles, meanders and zigzags; by the 8th century BC human figures returned, in scenes such as the funeral on the Dipylon Amphora. Contact with the Near East brought an "Orientalising" style in the 7th century BC, with animal friezes and monsters, led by Corinth.

In the black-figure technique, developed at Corinth and perfected in Athens, figures were painted in a slip that fired black, with details scratched through to the red clay and touched up in red and white. Masters such as Kleitias and Exekias made black-figure the dominant Athenian style until about 530 BC. Then Athenian potters invented red-figure, reversing the scheme: the background was painted black and the figures left in the red of the clay, with details drawn in fine lines. This freedom let painters such as Euphronios show anatomy, movement and emotion.

Many vases were made for the symposium and for funerals, and many were signed by their painters and potters. Athenian vases were exported widely, especially to Etruria. Production of fine figured pottery declined in the 4th century BC.

name: Greek sculpture

claims.text: Archaic kouroi derive their pose from Egyptian sculpture.
Greek marble sculpture was originally painted.
Most famous Greek bronzes are known only from Roman marble copies.
Contrapposto, the weight-shift pose, appears around 480 BC in works such as the Kritios Boy.

summary: The sculpture of the Greek world, from stiff Archaic kouroi to the idealised figures of the Classical age and the drama of Hellenistic art.
significance: Greek sculptors invented the naturalistic, idealised human figure that dominated Western art from Rome to the Renaissance and beyond.
body:
Large-scale stone sculpture appeared in Greece in the 7th century BC, influenced by Egypt. The Archaic period produced the *kouros*, a standing nude youth, and the *korē*, a clothed young woman, used as grave markers and offerings to the gods. They stand stiffly, left foot forward, with the faint "Archaic smile".

Around 480 BC sculptors broke with this formula. Works such as the Kritios Boy shift their weight onto one leg (contrapposto), and the body responds naturally. The bronze-casting of the Severe Style, seen in the Charioteer of Delphi and the Riace Bronzes, led to the High Classical art of Pheidias and the Parthenon sculptures, and Polykleitos' *Doryphoros*, built on ideal proportions. In the 4th century BC Praxiteles, Scopas and Lysippos made figures softer, more emotional and more varied; Praxiteles' Aphrodite of Knidos was the first monumental female nude.

Hellenistic sculpture after Alexander explored drama, suffering, old age and portraiture, in works such as the Pergamon Altar, the Dying Gaul, the Winged Victory of Samothrace and the Laocoön.

Two facts change how Greek sculpture should be imagined. It was painted, often brightly, and the white marble look comes from paint loss. And most famous bronzes were melted down; they survive mostly through Roman marble copies. Originals such as the Riace and Artemision bronzes show how much was lost.

name: Greek philosophy

claims.text: Greek philosophy is traditionally said to begin with Thales of Miletus in the early 6th century BC.
The Presocratics sought natural rather than mythological explanations of the world.
Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum were among the first lasting schools of higher learning.
Stoicism, Epicureanism and Scepticism were the leading philosophical schools of the Hellenistic age.

summary: The tradition of rational enquiry into nature, knowledge, ethics and politics that began in Ionia in the 6th century BC.
significance: The origin of Western philosophy and science: its questions, methods and schools shaped Roman, Islamic, medieval and modern thought.
body:
Greek philosophy began in the Ionian city of Miletus in the early 6th century BC, when Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes tried to explain the world in terms of natural substances and processes rather than the actions of gods. These early thinkers, the Presocratics, offered bold theories: Heraclitus' world of constant change, Parmenides' unchanging being, Pythagoras' cosmos of numbers, Empedocles' four elements and the atoms of Leucippus and Democritus.

In the 5th century BC attention turned to human affairs. The Sophists taught rhetoric and questioned whether morality was natural or merely conventional. Socrates, in Athens, cross-examined his fellow citizens about justice, courage and the good life, and was executed in 399 BC.

His pupil Plato founded the Academy around 387 BC and wrote dialogues developing the theory of Forms and the ideal state of the *Republic*. Plato's pupil Aristotle founded the Lyceum in 335 BC and wrote on logic, nature, ethics, politics and poetry, laying foundations for many later sciences.

After Alexander, philosophy became a guide to living well. The Stoics of Zeno taught virtue and acceptance of fate; Epicurus taught a calm life free from fear, based on atomism; the Sceptics, following Pyrrho, suspended judgement; and the Cynics, such as Diogenes, rejected social conventions. These schools continued into the Roman world and, with Plato and Aristotle, shaped philosophy for two thousand years.

name: Greek science and medicine

claims.text: Hippocratic medicine explained disease by natural causes rather than divine anger.
Euclid's Elements set out geometry as a deductive system from definitions and postulates.
Herophilus and Erasistratus performed human dissections at Alexandria in the 3rd century BC.
The Antikythera Mechanism shows geared astronomical calculating devices existed by the 2nd century BC.

summary: The mathematics, astronomy, medicine and natural science of the Greeks, which reached its height in Hellenistic Alexandria.
significance: The Greeks created the idea of science as explaining nature by reasoned argument and proof; their geometry, astronomy and medicine were the foundation of science until the 17th century.
body:
Greek science grew out of the same Ionian curiosity as philosophy. In the 6th century BC Thales and Anaximander sought natural explanations of the world, and Pythagoras and his followers found mathematical order in music and the heavens.

Medicine became rational in the 5th century BC with Hippocrates of Kos and the writings collected under his name, which explained illness by natural causes such as diet, climate and the balance of bodily fluids, and stressed careful observation of patients. Aristotle, in the 4th century BC, founded systematic biology through his study of animals.

The great age of Greek science was the Hellenistic period, centred on the Museum and Library of Alexandria. Euclid organised geometry into a deductive system; Archimedes calculated areas and volumes, founded hydrostatics and built war machines; Apollonius wrote on conic sections. Aristarchus proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun; Eratosthenes measured the Earth; Hipparchus catalogued the stars and discovered the precession of the equinoxes. At Alexandria Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies, discovering the nerves and studying the brain and heart. Engineers such as Ctesibius built water clocks and pumps, and the Antikythera Mechanism shows how sophisticated Greek instruments could be.

Greek science was largely theoretical, with little systematic experiment. But through Ptolemy and Galen in the Roman period, and Arabic and Latin translators afterwards, it shaped the science of the Islamic world and Europe until the Scientific Revolution.

name: Trade and the Greek economy

claims.text: Most Greeks worked the land, growing mainly cereals, olives and vines.
Athens depended on grain imported from the Black Sea region in the Classical period.
Coinage spread through the Greek cities within decades of its invention in Lydia.
Transport amphorae allow archaeologists to trace the trade in wine and olive oil.

summary: How the Greeks made a living: farming, crafts, trade by sea, slavery and the spread of coined money.
significance: Greek trade networks and coinage knit the Mediterranean together and spread Greek goods, wine, olive oil and culture far beyond Greece.
body:
Most Greeks lived by farming. Greece's thin soils and dry summers suited the "Mediterranean triad" of wheat or barley, olives and grapes, along with sheep and goats. Most farms were small family holdings, as Hesiod's *Works and Days* describes, though the rich owned larger estates worked by slaves or tenants.

Because good land was limited, Greek cities looked to the sea. From the 8th century BC colonies and trading posts — Al Mina in Syria, Pithekoussai in Italy, Naukratis in Egypt — linked Greece with the Near East, Egypt, Italy and the Black Sea. Greeks exported wine, olive oil, fine pottery and metalwork, and imported grain, timber, metals and slaves. Transport jars (*amphorae*), stamped with their city's mark, let archaeologists trace this trade. By the 5th century BC Athens depended on grain shipped from the Black Sea, which made control of the Hellespont a matter of survival.

Coinage, invented in Lydia in the late 7th century BC, spread rapidly through the Greek cities, making trade, taxation and the payment of soldiers and officials easier. Athens' silver owls, minted from the Laurion mines, became the most trusted currency of the Classical world.

Craftsmen, many of them resident foreigners or slaves, worked in small workshops. Markets (*agorai*), harbours such as Piraeus, banks and maritime loans developed. In the Hellenistic period royal economies, such as that of Ptolemaic Egypt, operated on a far larger scale.

name: Mystery cults

claims.text: Initiates into the Eleusinian Mysteries were forbidden to reveal what they saw, and the secret was largely kept.
The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is the founding myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
Mystery initiation offered a better fate after death.
The Derveni Papyrus preserves a commentary on an Orphic theogony.

summary: Secret religious rites, open to those who chose to be initiated, that promised a closer bond with the gods and a better life after death.
significance: The most personal side of Greek religion, offering individual hope beyond death; the Eleusinian Mysteries drew initiates for a thousand years.
body:
Alongside the public worship of the city's gods, many Greeks sought initiation into "mysteries" (*mystēria*), rites revealed only to those who had been initiated (*mystai*). Initiates swore to keep the rites secret, and they largely did, so much about them remains unknown.

The most famous were the Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and her daughter Persephone, celebrated at Eleusis near Athens from at least the 7th century BC. Their founding story, told in the Homeric *Hymn to Demeter*, is Persephone's seizure by Hades and her return each year. Each autumn initiates walked in procession from Athens to Eleusis and, inside the great hall of initiation, saw sacred things revealed by torchlight. Initiation was open to men and women, free and slave, Greek speakers of any city, and was believed to bring a happier lot after death. Its rites continued until the Christian emperor Theodosius I suppressed pagan cult in AD 392.

Other mysteries included those of the Great Gods on Samothrace, believed to protect sailors, and of Dionysus. The Orphic movement, linked to the mythical singer Orpheus, taught that the soul was immortal and could be purified through a special way of life; gold leaves buried with the dead give instructions for the journey to the underworld, and the Derveni Papyrus preserves a commentary on an Orphic poem.

In the Roman period mystery cults of Isis, Mithras and others spread widely.

name: Leagues and alliances

claims.text: The Peloponnesian League, led by Sparta, took shape in the 6th century BC.
The Delian League was founded in 478 BC under Athenian leadership.
The Achaean and Aetolian Leagues were federal states with shared citizenship and federal assemblies.
The Achaean League was dissolved by Rome after the war of 146 BC.

summary: The alliances and federations through which Greek city-states combined for war and, later, shared government.
significance: Leagues shaped the great wars of Greece and, in the Hellenistic federal states, produced one of antiquity's most advanced experiments in shared government.
body:
Greek city-states prized their independence but constantly joined together for security. Most leagues were military alliances (*symmachiai*) led by a strong city. The Peloponnesian League, formed under Spartan leadership in the 6th century BC, bound most Peloponnesian cities to follow Sparta in war. The Delian League, founded in 478 BC to fight Persia, was led by Athens and became an Athenian empire. Their rivalry produced the Peloponnesian War. In the 4th century BC Athens founded a second, milder league, and Philip II united the Greek states in the League of Corinth in 337 BC under his leadership.

Other leagues were regional federations of neighbouring communities sharing an identity. The Boeotian League, dominated by Thebes, had a federal council and army. The Thessalian and Arcadian Leagues were similar.

In the Hellenistic period, two federal states became major powers: the Aetolian League in central Greece and the Achaean League in the Peloponnese. They had a shared citizenship, federal assemblies and elected generals, while member cities kept local self-government. Under leaders such as Aratus and Philopoemen, the Achaean League united much of the Peloponnese, and the historian Polybius, himself an Achaean statesman, admired it. The framers of the United States Constitution studied these federations.

Rome first allied with and then broke up the leagues. After the Achaean revolt of 146 BC, Rome destroyed Corinth and dissolved the League.

name: Macedon

claims.text: Macedon was ruled by the Argead dynasty, which claimed descent from Heracles and from Argos.
The Argead kings were admitted to the Olympic Games as Greeks after Alexander I proved his Argive descent.
Whether the ancient Macedonian language was a Greek dialect is debated, though recent evidence favours it.
Rome abolished the Macedonian monarchy after Pydna in 168 BC.

summary: The kingdom on the northern edge of the Greek world that, under Philip II and Alexander, conquered Greece and the Persian Empire.
significance: The power that ended the age of independent city-states and carried Greek culture from the Balkans to India.
body:
Macedon lay in the plains and mountains around the Thermaic Gulf, north of Thessaly and Mount Olympus. Its lowlands were rich in grain and horses, its uplands in timber and, later, gold and silver. Unlike the southern city-states, it remained a kingdom, ruled from about 700 BC by the Argead dynasty, which claimed descent from Heracles and from Argos. The capital was Aigai (Vergina), later moved to Pella around 400 BC; Aigai remained the royal burial place.

Southern Greeks often looked down on the Macedonians as semi-barbarian, though their kings took part in Greek culture: Alexander I competed at Olympia, and Archelaus invited Euripides and other artists to his court. Whether the Macedonian language was a dialect of Greek is debated; recent inscriptions favour a Greek dialect. Macedonian society was dominated by a warrior aristocracy, the king's Companions.

For long a weak kingdom troubled by neighbours, Macedon was transformed by Philip II (359–336 BC), who built a professional army armed with the long sarissa and mastered Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire. After Alexander's death, Macedon itself was fought over until the Antigonid dynasty secured it in the 270s BC.

Rome defeated Macedon in a series of wars and, after Pydna in 168 BC, abolished the monarchy. It became a Roman province in 148 BC.

name: Attica

claims.text: Attica, about 2,500 square kilometres, formed the single territory of the polis of Athens.
Attica's silver mines at Laurion financed the Athenian fleet and coinage.
Athenian tradition credited Theseus with uniting the villages of Attica into one state.

summary: The triangular peninsula of central Greece that formed the territory of Athens.
significance: The homeland of Athenian democracy, whose silver mines, harbours and farms made Athens the leading power of Classical Greece.
body:
Attica is the triangular peninsula of central Greece pointing south-east into the Aegean, about 2,500 square kilometres, bounded by the mountains of Kithairon and Parnes on the north and by the sea on its other sides. Unusually for Greece, the whole region formed a single city-state: Athens. Athenians credited the hero Theseus with uniting its villages into one state.

Its landscape was mountainous, with small plains around Athens, Eleusis and Marathon, thin soil and dry summers better suited to olives, vines and figs than to grain. Its mountains supplied the fine marble of Pentelikon and Hymettos, used for the Parthenon, and the clay of its potters. In the south, the silver mines of Laurion financed Themistocles' fleet in 483 BC and the coinage of Athens, worked by thousands of slaves.

Cleisthenes' reforms of 508/7 BC divided Attica into about 140 local communities, the demes, grouped into city, coast and inland zones, which became the basis of citizenship. Many Athenians lived in these rural demes rather than in the city itself.
