Attica's famous places include the battlefield of Marathon, the sanctuary of Eleusis, the temple of Poseidon at Sounion and the harbour of Piraeus. In the Peloponnesian War Spartan armies repeatedly ravaged its countryside, forcing its people behind the walls of Athens.

name: Boeotia

claims.text: Boeotia was organised as the Boeotian League, usually dominated by Thebes.
So many battles were fought there that Epaminondas called it the "dancing floor of Ares".
The poets Hesiod and Pindar were Boeotians.

summary: The fertile region of central Greece north-west of Attica, dominated by Thebes and the scene of many of Greece's decisive battles.
significance: A rich farming land and the home of Hesiod and Pindar, whose plains were the battlefield of Greece from Plataea to Chaeronea.
body:
Boeotia is the region of central Greece lying between Attica to the south-east and Phocis to the west, with fertile plains around Thebes and the great lake of Copais (drained only in modern times). In the Bronze Age it was home to the powerful Mycenaean centres of Thebes, Orchomenos and the vast fortress of Gla, which helped drain the Copais basin.

In the historical period its cities were joined in the Boeotian League, a federation usually dominated by Thebes, with a federal council and army. Other Boeotian cities, such as Plataea and Orchomenos, often resented Theban control; Plataea sided with Athens and fought beside it at Marathon.

Athenians mocked Boeotians as dull farmers, but the region produced the poets Hesiod, whose *Works and Days* describes life at Ascra, and Pindar of Thebes, as well as the poet Corinna. Its open plains made it the battlefield of Greece, which Epaminondas reportedly called "the dancing floor of Ares": Plataea (479 BC), Delium (424 BC), Leuctra (371 BC) and Chaeronea (338 BC) were all fought there.

Under Epaminondas and Pelopidas, Boeotia under Thebes became the leading power in Greece after Leuctra. Its independence ended with Philip II's victory at Chaeronea and Alexander's destruction of Thebes in 335 BC.

name: Ionia

claims.text: Ionia was settled by Greek speakers in the centuries after about 1050 BC.
Twelve Ionian cities formed a religious league centred on the Panionion sanctuary.
Greek natural philosophy began in Ionia, at Miletus, in the 6th century BC.
The Ionian Revolt against Persia began in 499 BC.

summary: The central west coast of Asia Minor and its islands, settled by Greeks after the Bronze Age — birthplace of Greek philosophy and science.
significance: The most advanced region of the Archaic Greek world: the home of Homeric epic, the first philosophers and the revolt that began the Persian Wars.
body:
Ionia was the central part of the west coast of Asia Minor, modern Turkey, with the nearby islands of Chios and Samos. Greek speakers settled it in the centuries after about 1050 BC, in the movement later remembered as the Ionian migration. Twelve Ionian cities — including Miletus, Ephesus, Samos, Chios, Phocaea and Colophon — formed a religious league that met at the Panionion sanctuary.

Ionia sat at the meeting point of the Greek world and the kingdoms of Anatolia and the Near East, and in the Archaic period it was the most prosperous and creative part of the Greek world. The Homeric epics probably took shape here. Ionian cities founded colonies around the Black Sea and as far as France. At Miletus in the 6th century BC Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes began Greek philosophy and science, followed by Heraclitus of Ephesus; Hecataeus pioneered geography and history; and Ionian architects built the first great Ionic temples.

The Ionian cities fell under Lydian rule and, after 546 BC, under Persia. Their revolt in 499 BC, supported by Athens, led to the Persian invasions of Greece. Freed after 479 BC, they joined the Delian League, but were handed back to Persia by the King's Peace of 387 BC. Alexander freed them again in 334 BC, and Ionian cities such as Ephesus flourished in the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

name: Magna Graecia

claims.text: Greek colonists founded cities in southern Italy and Sicily from about 750 BC.
Pythagoras founded his community at Croton in southern Italy.
Greek culture in Italy strongly influenced the Etruscans and the Romans.

summary: The Greek cities of southern Italy and, in a wider sense, Sicily — the rich western frontier of the Greek world.
significance: Wealthy cities that rivalled mainland Greece, produced philosophers and scientists, and passed Greek culture to the Etruscans and Romans.
body:
"Magna Graecia" (Great Greece) was the Roman name for the Greek cities of southern Italy, and is often extended to include Sicily. Greek settlers came from the mid-8th century BC: Euboeans to Pithekoussai and Cumae near Naples, Achaeans to Sybaris and Croton, Spartans to Taras (Taranto), Corinthians to Syracuse, and many others. The land was fertile and the cities grew rich; Sybaris became a byword for luxury.

The western Greeks made major contributions to Greek culture. Pythagoras founded his community at Croton; Parmenides and Zeno taught at Elea; Empedocles came from Akragas in Sicily; and Archimedes lived at Syracuse. The Doric temples of Paestum, Akragas and Selinous are among the best preserved in the Greek world. Syracuse, under its tyrants, became one of the great powers of the Mediterranean and defeated the Athenian invasion of 415–413 BC.

The western Greeks fought constantly with each other, with the Italian peoples around them, and in Sicily with Carthage. Through trade and contact, they passed the alphabet, gods, art and ideas to the Etruscans and to Rome.

In the 3rd century BC Rome absorbed the cities of southern Italy, after defeating Pyrrhus of Epirus, who had come to help Taras, and took Sicily from Carthage. Syracuse fell in 212 BC. Greek remained widely spoken in the region for centuries.
